title: The Big Bang
subtitle: 13.8 billion years
subject: sciences
description: 13.8 billion years ago, the universe began to expand. It's not a bomb in a vacuum: it's space itself that is growing.

hero.hook: The Big Bang is not an explosion in space. It is the space that begins to grow.

blocks.text: **13.8 billion years ago**, everything that exists today was concentrated in an extremely dense and hot state. Scientists sometimes call this beginning a [[singularity]]: a point where density and temperature are so extreme that our usual laws are no longer sufficient to describe the situation.

Then the universe begins to expand. It's not a bomb that throws matter into a void that's already there. It is **space-time**, the fabric that unites space and time, which grows, taking matter with it. This story continues today.

sections.title: Not an explosion in the void

blocks.text: The name **“Big Bang”** is confusing. We often imagine fireworks in the middle of an empty room. But before this event, there is neither room nor outside. Space and time as we know them begin with him. Ask “what was there before?” » therefore becomes very delicate: the “before” no longer has the same meaning.

blocks.caption: The expansion of the Universe since the Big Bang.

blocks.text: The term "Big Bang" was coined in **1949** by the British astrophysicist **Fred Hoyle**, who did not believe in it. He wanted to laugh at the idea. The nickname stuck.

To imagine expansion, imagine dots drawn on a balloon. When you inflate the balloon, each point moves away from the others. No point on the surface is “the center.” In the universe, it's a bit the same idea: the **galaxies**, immense groups of stars, are moving away from each other because the space between them is stretching.

In **1929**, the American astronomer **Edwin Hubble** observed that the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it moves away. The universe is therefore not fixed: it is growing. This is **Hubble's law**, the relationship between distance and escape velocity of galaxies.

In **1965**, two engineers, **Arno Penzias** and **Robert Wilson**, picked up a radio crackle coming from everywhere. This is the [[The cosmic microwave background (CMB)]]: a sort of thermal echo from the young universe, emitted when light was able to circulate freely for the first time, approximately **380, 000 years** after the beginning.
A small part of the “snow” from old, poorly tuned analog televisions came from this cosmic background.

Third pillar: the proportions of light elements. Calculations predict approximately **75%** of hydrogen and **25%** of helium formed in the first few minutes. Observations confirm these figures. This is the [[primordial nucleosynthesis]], the factory of the first atomic nuclei in the minutes following the Big Bang.

Just after the beginning, the universe goes through a phase of **inflation**, an extremely rapid expansion in a fraction of a second. Then, around **3 minutes**, **protons** and **neutrons**, particles which make up atomic nuclei, assemble into the first nuclei. For a long time, the universe remains like an opaque fog: light does not travel freely.

Around **380,000 years**, the **electrons**, light particles which orbit around the nuclei, join the nuclei to form neutral atoms. The light is released: it is the emission of the diffuse background. The first stars were born much later, around **200 million years** later. Our Sun only appeared **4.6 billion years ago**, from material recycled by ancient stars.
If the history of the universe took place in one year, the Big Bang would take place on January 1 at midnight, and humanity would not appear until December 31 at 11:52 p.m. .

For a long time, people wondered whether gravity would eventually slow the expansion. In **1998**, the observation of distant , star explosions used as distance markers, shows the opposite: the . A mysterious **dark energy**, a repulsive force that pushes galaxies away, would seem to push this distance away, and would represent approximately **68%** of the contents of the universe. Ordinary matter, that of which we are made, would only make about **5 %**. [[supernovas]] [[accelerated expansion of the universe]]

If this acceleration continues, the universe could trend towards extreme cooling, sometimes nicknamed **Big Freeze**, the end by cold. One thing is certain: what we see is only a portion of the whole. As light travels towards us, space continues to stretch.

The Big Bang, **13.8 billion years ago**, is not an explosion in empty space: it is the expansion of space itself, confirmed by the flight of galaxies, the cosmic microwave background and the proportions of hydrogen and helium.
